consecrate

/KON-sih-krayt/ · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Consecrate means to dedicate something as sacred in a formal, solemn ceremony.

The village elders gathered at dawn to consecrate the new well to the memory of the flood's victims.

Example

The families had carried stones from the ruined schoolhouse across three valleys. When the small mountain shrine was finally complete, the eldest villager climbed up at first light with salt, song, and a handful of ash from the old hearth. In a short ceremony, she consecrated the shrine to the children lost in the avalanche. From that morning on, travelers left wildflowers there, and no one ever pitched a tent within its low stone walls. Ordinary rock had been formally set apart for something solemn.

The ceremony that formally sets the shrine apart for a solemn memorial purpose — after which everyone treats the ground differently — is what it means to consecrate it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

bless: Bless means to call down divine favor or protection on someone or something, often with a short prayer or gesture. Consecrate goes further and is more formal: in a solemn ceremony, a person with authority sets a thing apart as sacred from then on. A meal can be blessed in a moment; a chapel is consecrated for good.

enshrine: Enshrine means to preserve something as precious and untouchable - relics kept in a shrine, or rights enshrined in a constitution. Consecrate is the formal, solemn act that first declares a thing sacred. Enshrining protects what is already treasured; consecrating is the ceremony that sets it apart to begin with.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

desecrate: to treat a sacred place with violent disrespect

defile: to make dirty or impure

Where it sits · how deeply something is made holy — dedicate → consecrate → sanctify

dedicate vs. consecrate: Dedicate is the everyday, weaker cousin — you can dedicate a book, a bench, or a season to almost anything; consecrate adds formal ceremony and a holy or solemn purpose.

sanctify vs. consecrate: Sanctify is stronger still: it claims the thing has actually been made holy, while consecrate emphasizes the formal act of setting it apart.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: together; thoroughly

Root — secr

Root — secr: holy (Latin sacer)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending

Put it together

Put it together: Consecrate comes from Latin consecrare: con- (thoroughly) plus sacrare, 'to make holy,' from sacer (holy). To consecrate is literally to make something thoroughly sacred. The same root gives English sacred and sacrifice (literally 'to make holy'), and its dark twin desecrate — to strip that holiness away.

Use the root in a new word: sacred

Use the root in a new word: sacred: In that newsroom the noon deadline is sacrosanct, whatever else the day brings.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, ceremonial

Consecrate almost always involves a formal act or ceremony — a person with authority deliberately sets something apart. You consecrate ground, buildings, or even a life to a purpose; for casual commitments ('she dedicated her weekend to studying'), dedicate is the right register, not consecrate.
